vignette:
Mateo, a 53-year-old tax consultant, had always prided himself on his meticulous nature and calm demeanor, qualities that served him well in his demanding profession. That changed irrevocably five years ago during what should have been a routine evening. He had been walking home after a community meeting, a local gathering discussing zoning changes, when the atmosphere suddenly shifted. Police, who had been monitoring the protest, escalated their presence. A minor scuffle broke out further down the street, and before Mateo could process what was happening, he found himself caught in a surge of bodies. He was shoved to the ground, his head hitting the pavement, and then the blows began. He remembered the sickening thud of a baton against his ribs, the searing pain in his arm as it was twisted, and the metallic tang of blood in his mouth. What truly haunted him, however, was the sight of others around him, people he recognised from the neighbourhood, being similarly brutalised, some bleeding profusely from head wounds, their faces contorted in agony. The screams, the flashes of uniform, and the raw, unadulterated pain became indelibly etched into his mind.

In the years that followed, Mateo found his world shrinking. The once minor aches and pains he experienced in his body now carried a terrifying significance. A dull throb in his wrist, the one that had been fractured that night, could instantly transport him back to the ground, reliving the terror and helplessness. He’d feel the impact of the baton, the cold pavement against his cheek, and a wave of nausea would wash over him. Similarly, the sight of any visible injury on another person, even a child’s scraped knee in the park, could trigger a visceral reaction. His stomach would clench, his breath would catch, and the vivid images of the bleeding faces he’d witnessed during the incident would flood his mind, leaving him shaken and needing to distance himself. He also found himself constantly bombarded by reminders of victims, whether it was a news report about a crime or even a fictional character enduring hardship on television; a profound sense of despair would overwhelm him, solidifying his belief that the world was a dangerous and unjust place.

His professional life as a tax consultant, which often required him to visit clients at their offices or other unfamiliar locations, became increasingly challenging. Mateo developed an intense aversion to going to unfamiliar places, convinced he couldn’t adequately assess the danger lurking within them. He began to decline new clients if their premises were in parts of the city he didn’t know, or if he couldn't easily map out the surrounding area online beforehand. This decision, made out of a desperate need for perceived safety, had slowly but surely begun to impact his income and the growth of his practice, leaving him feeling professionally stagnant. When he did venture out, or even when he was simply walking down a familiar street, he found himself compulsively looking behind him, his heart pounding, certain that someone might be following him, that the threat was always imminent. Before he could feel comfortable in any new environment – a restaurant, a client’s waiting room, even a friend’s new apartment – his eyes would instinctively scan for escape routes, mentally cataloguing exits and potential pathways to safety. He couldn’t relax until he had a plan, a way out, should the worst happen again.

As these coping mechanisms solidified into habits, Mateo’s inner world became increasingly bleak. He had come to believe that there was something intrinsically wrong with him, something about his presence or his actions that night that had made the event happen. This corrosive self-blame, a deeply personal interpretation of the trauma, fostered a profound sense of isolation. He felt utterly set apart from others, convinced that no one could truly understand the weight of his experience or the shame he carried. His divorce, which predated the incident but had left him already feeling somewhat adrift, now felt amplified by this profound loneliness. The cumulative burden of constant vigilance, the fear, and the self-reproach had led him to a dark place where he frequently questioned the value of his existence. He was not sure his life was worth living anymore, a chilling thought that often accompanied him through sleepless nights. It was this creeping despair, this profound sense of meaninglessness, that finally propelled him to seek help, a desperate attempt to find a way out of the suffocating cage his life had become, though he was terrified that revisiting the past might only confirm his deepest fears about himself.
